claim: Among the estimated 1.5 million people who died from TB in 2013, 360,000 were HIV co-infected.

claim: Among the estimated 1.5 million people who died from TB in 2013, 200,000 cases were caused by multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB).

claim: Until the late 1980s, reports of MDR-TB were rare.

claim: The MDR-TB burden surged concurrently with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) pandemic.
source: The MDR-TB burden surged concurrently with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) pandemic and most reported early MDR-TB outbreaks mainly affected HIV co-infected individuals in hospitals and prisons (Small et al., 1993; Wells et al., 2007; Ritacco et al., 1997).

claim: HIV infection renders people more susceptible to develop active TB by weakening their immune system.
source: Not only does HIV infection render people more susceptible to develop active TB by weakening their immune system, but anti-TB drugs can also directly interfere with antiretroviral treatment.

claim: Anti-TB drugs can directly interfere with antiretroviral treatment.
source: Not only does HIV infection render people more susceptible to develop active TB by weakening their immune system, but anti-TB drugs can also directly interfere with antiretroviral treatment.

claim: Rifampicin (RIF) significantly lowers serum concentrations of HIV protease and reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
source: Rifampicin (RIF), one of the cornerstones in anti-TB therapy, has been shown to significantly lower serum concentrations of HIV protease and reverse transcriptase inhibitors (Burman et al., 1999; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burman et al., 1999; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1998

claim: HIV co-infection is associated with malabsorption of anti-TB drugs.
source: To make matters worse, HIV co-infection is also associated with malabsorption of anti-TB drugs. This pattern is particularly pronounced for RIF, but seems to hold true for most anti-TB drugs (Patel et al., 1995; Peloquin et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Patel et al., 1995; Peloquin et al., 1993

claim: The pattern of malabsorption of anti-TB drugs in HIV co-infection is particularly pronounced for RIF.

claim: Resistance mutations generally entail a fitness cost to the bacterium, at least initially.
source: First, as resistance mutations generally entail a fitness cost to the bacterium (at least initially), some resistant strains might be more successful in HIV+ hosts with weakened immunity leading to a reduced selective pressure on the bacillus.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the manuscript

claim: Some resistant strains might be more successful in HIV+ hosts with weakened immunity leading to a reduced selective pressure on the bacillus.
source: First, as resistance mutations generally entail a fitness cost to the bacterium (at least initially), some resistant strains might be more successful in HIV+ hosts with weakened immunity leading to a reduced selective pressure on the bacillus.

evidence: Supported by citations to Bradford et al., 1996; Burman et al., 2006; Li et al., 2005; Porco et al., 2013

claim: HIV has been a driver of increased TB incidence globally.
